questions.prompt: What is the single most commonly botched step in BEC response?
options: Resetting the password without revoking sessions, leaving existing refresh tokens valid so the attacker retains access
Collecting message trace data too early
Contacting the bank before completing technical scoping
questions.explanation: A GUI-only password reset does not invalidate existing refresh tokens. Without explicit session revocation, the attacker continues working through tokens issued before the reset.

questions.prompt: Why must attacker-registered MFA methods be checked during initial containment?
options: MFA methods expire automatically after 24 hours
An attacker who enrolled their own authenticator retains access through your password reset
MFA registration is never possible for an attacker
Only Global Admins can register MFA methods
questions.explanation: Enrolling an additional MFA method is a persistence technique that survives credential rotation entirely, so enumeration and removal must happen as part of the reset rather than afterward.

questions.prompt: Which operation is key to making a defensible statement about what data was actually exposed in a BEC?
questions.explanation: MailItemsAccessed is what distinguishes 'the account was accessed' from a supportable statement about which mail items the attacker actually read.

questions.prompt: Why do OAuth consent grants need reviewing even after a full password reset and session revocation?
options: They do not; the reset covers them
OAuth grants survive password resets entirely and are a frequently-missed persistence path
They expire after one hour automatically
They only apply to on-premises accounts
questions.explanation: A granted OAuth application retains its own access independent of the user's password and sessions, making it durable persistence unless explicitly revoked.
